runs.text: ſom dos pees do que baila. ¶

lines.note: Continues f435's threefold musical harmony with the sound of the dancer's feet. Pees and baila restore letters lost by OCR; the preceding page's catchword repeats ſom.
Ga soro completes the Japanese example: the three elements agree or come into alignment. The Portuguese continues the description of their musical agreement.

runs.text: ſom, ou compaßo. ¶ Itẽ, per met.

lines.note: Completes agreement in sound or rhythm, then introduces a metaphorical use. The repeated Sanpiǒ- has a visible caron, not the OCR circumflex.
Completes sanpyoshi ga sorota, the desirable elements having come together. The Portuguese describes things arriving together opportunely.

runs.text: propoſito, ou a pedir por boca.

lines.note: Completes the metaphor as things coming just as desired. The idiom a pedir por boca is retained rather than translated inside the canonical transcription.
The expression imagines mountains made into writing pens or brushes. Sanpit preserves the printed final checked consonant rather than expanding it into a syllable.
Completes the image with the sea made into inkwells, then begins an example saying even such means would be insufficient.

runs.text: Couſa que não ſe pode de-

lines.note: Oyobigatashi completes the expression of insufficiency. The Portuguese begins describing something that cannot be fully explained or set down in writing.

runs.text: clarar, nem eſcreuer, & eſgotar por pena.

lines.note: Completes declarar and says the subject cannot be exhausted by the pen. This makes sense of the extravagant mountains-and-sea image.
Sanpuku is illustrated by kiuka sanpuku, the hottest part of summer. The caron over u is preserved in the Japanese example.
Completes the definition as the most sultry time of summer. Calmoso concerns heat here, not merely calmness.

runs.text: Sanpugiô. i, Xi, facu, giôni tonzuru coto.

lines.note: The Japanese paraphrase introduces indulgence in the three activities explained below. The headword and explanatory i, are upright; the OCR's isolated italic p is spurious.

runs.text: Darſe muito ao vinho, jogo, & molheres.

lines.note: Explains the three indulgences as wine, gambling, and women. This supplies the semantic control for the preceding Japanese phrase without modernizing its spellings.

runs.text: Ir à Tera, ou Ermida dos Camis. Vt,

lines.note: Sankei means visiting a temple or shrine. Tera and Camis are Japanese religious terms embedded in the Portuguese definition; Vt, introduces the example below.
Tera e sankei suru illustrates making a temple visit. The printed r in Teraye corrects OCR Tetaye and matches Tera in the preceding gloss.
Sankyo is dwelling in the mountains or wilderness, paraphrased as yama ni iru. The Portuguese sentence continues on the next row.
Completes the alternative dwelling-place as the mountains. It remains attached to the preceding sankyo definition.

runs.text: Ermitão, ou homem que faz pe-

lines.note: Sankyojin is a hermit or a person performing penance. The Portuguese homem has a worn h, not the OCR b.
Completes penitencia and places the ascetic practice in the wilderness. The division pe-/nitencia is preserved physically.
Sankyonin is given as equivalent to sankyojin, the hermit defined above. Idem refers to that immediately preceding entry.
Sankirai is identified by the historical Portuguese materia-medica name pao da china. The example starts an expression about drinking a preparation of it.
Nomu completes drinking the water prepared from that material. The gloss describes usage without establishing a precise modern botanical identification.
Sanka means mountain flowers. The Portuguese offers roses or flowers of the wilderness, with the location completed below.
Completes the description of wild flowers. This single-word row belongs to sanqua.
Sankwai concerns familiar conversation or association. Enlargement establishes the printed v in Mairivǒ, not OCR b; fa- begins familiar.

runs.text: miliar. ¶ Item, Encontrarſe, ou verſe com

lines.note: Completes familiar intercourse, then adds meeting or seeing someone. The second definition leads into the following example.
Completes meeting someone and illustrates it with sankwai suru. The terminal OCR i after suru is absent from the scan.
Sankwanrei names three noble families of Japan. The continuous headword and Iapão correct the OCR split and the mistaken initial t.

Lists the three families named in the Portuguese definition. The worn letters in Fataqeyama are read with the surrounding name and visible q descender; these are embedded names, not independent headwords.
Sankwo is paraphrased as three emperors or sovereigns. The Portuguese identifies them as three rulers of China in the continuation.
Names the three Chinese rulers. Enlargement supports the circumflex in Xinuô, distinct from the clear caron in Quǒei; the printed names are not modernized.
This separate sankwo means three lights or luminaries. Its Japanese paraphrase distinguishes it from the preceding three-sovereigns entry.

runs.text: ou lumieiras. ſ. Sol, lũa, eſtrelas. Vt,

lines.note: Names the three luminaries as sun, moon, and stars. The example's final c-like sort in Iic- is retained after enlargement rather than silently supplied as an expected t; the reading remains a nonblocking caveat.
Completes the example referring to the sun, moon, and stars as the three lights. The preceding divided form is interpreted with this list, without altering its anomalous printed consonant.
Sanrai means three adorations or reverences. The scan distinctly appears to print cu where ou is expected; the anomaly is preserved, and Vi- begins the cross-reference below.
De completes Vide, directing the reader to Sanpai. The Japanese reference is upright within the Portuguese apparatus.
Sanran is a mountain squall, paraphrased as yama arashi. The Portuguese describes a gust of wind coming from the mountains.
Completes the mountain-wind definition. This short continuation remains its own body row.
This sanran denotes scattering in disorder. The gloss first applies it to falling leaves, continuing with flowers below.

runs.text: das aruores, ou flores em quantidade eſpalhã-

lines.note: Adds flowers falling in quantity and scattering. The stray OCR l after ou is absent; the nasal abbreviation in eſpalhã- is retained.

runs.text: do ſe por diuerſas partes. ¶ Itẽ, Modo de ſe

lines.note: Completes spreading into different places, then introduces disordered dispersal of people. Modo corrects the OCR's Moao.
Describes people scattering and fleeing without order. The printed eſpalhar has no final e before its comma, correcting the draft.
Kokoro sanran suru describes distraction of the mind or heart. The verb is ſuru, not furu, and co- continues into coração.
Completes coração and the example of mental distraction. It does not begin an independent entry.
The Japanese synonym kiji identifies a pheasant, loosely glossed as a wild hen. The final headword mark is read as a caron with a faint left arm; the upright S. marks written usage.

Mairi tçuranaru denotes coming in an ordered line, matching Portuguese ir em fieira. The final headword sort is damaged: its surviving head and curved foot favour t, hence Sanret, not Sanrei. The supplied NINJAL entry independently supports Sanret and explicitly notes the poorly legible final t; the literal Portuguese fieira is retained.
Completes the definition as many people going together in order. The final row is ordinary body text above the bottom rule.

runs.text: Certo lugar a baixo dos joelhos onde ſe

lines.note: Sanri names a particular place below the knees. The historical definition introduces the heat treatment described on the next row.

runs.text: dão botões de fogo na canela da perna.

lines.note: Completes the description of applying small burning points on the shin. This is the source's historical account, not a treatment instruction added by the reviewer.

runs.text: Liuros que tratão da arte militar.

lines.note: Sanryaku is described as books treating the military arts. The verb is tratão, not the OCR's trutão.
Sanrin joins the ideas of mountains and woods. The Portuguese lists wild vegetation and bamboo thickets, continuing after a visible comma rather than the draft's full stop.
Completes the definition with woodland in the mountains. This is another gloss of sanrin, not an independent Japanese example.
Sanro means a mountain path, explicitly paraphrased by yama and michi. The headword has no long-vowel mark in this entry.

runs.text: Homem que habita nos matos. Vt,

lines.note: Sanro with a caron denotes a wilderness dweller. Ya- begins the paired rural-and-mountain-dweller example below.
Completes the statement that country and mountain folk all rejoice. Both long-o marks in the Japanese continuation are carons.

runs.text: do campo, & dos montes todos ſe alegram.

lines.note: Completes the Portuguese translation: all the rustic people of fields and mountains are glad. It confirms the coordination in the Japanese example.
Sanro with a circumflex denotes entering religious seclusion. The initial syllable reads San-, not Sin-; Tera is a Japanese term within the Portuguese explanation.
Completes going to a temple or hermitage to shut oneself away or remain in retreat. The two infinitival descriptions explain mairi komoru.
Sanron is identified as a particular Japanese religious school. The source does not elaborate its doctrines here.
Sansai comprises heaven, earth, and humanity. Homẽs restores the h misread by OCR while retaining the printed nasal abbreviation.
Sanson is a mountain settlement, paraphrased by yama and mura. The Portuguese location continues on the next line.
Completes the mountain-village definition and adds the upright written-usage label S.
Sansu concerns calculation and counting. The paired Japanese verbs introduce the two corresponding Portuguese infinitives across this break.
Completes counting and adds the upright written-usage label S. The word remains a continuation of sansu.
Sansui is mountain water, explained with yama and mizzu. The doubled z is preserved as part of the Japanese romanization.
Santo means three replies. The source's repoſtas is retained without inserting an extra s; the upright Sã- begins a divided cross-reference to Sanmon.
Completes the cross-reference Sã-/mon, whose nasal abbreviation is not expanded in the text. This row contains the reference target, not a fresh headword.
Santo designates the community of Mount Hiei monks. The headword's first vowel reads a, not OCR i; the printed unaccented ending is retained.
Completes the description as monks of rank at Mount Hiei. Fiyenoyama is a Japanese place name embedded in the Portuguese gloss.
Santo here is a mountain summit. The synonym itadaqi includes the t lost by OCR; cu- begins the Portuguese cume below.
Completes cume do monte, the summit of a mountain. It remains physically separate from the preceding row.
This separate santo means winter. The printed n in Inuerno corrects the OCR omission while preserving historical u for consonantal v.
Sanu is mountain rain, paraphrased by yama and ame. The final printed v, misread as o, is retained rather than modernized to u.
Sanwo is an old man living in the mountains. Voqina represents okina; the scan supports n rather than the OCR r, and Velho replaces Veſho.
Completes the location of the old man's dwelling. The short row closes sanvo and is not page furniture.

Sanuqi yẽza names a Sanuki rush seat. The Portuguese begins a comparison with a mat; the scan supports the nasal mark in yẽza, the double-s sort in Aßẽto, and como rather than the OCR's cemo. The close join debunho is retained.

runs.text: cho, ou tanho raſo q̃ ſe faz no reino de

lines.note: Completes capacho and describes a low tanho made in Sanuki. The scan supports tanho, raſo and no; q̃ remains abbreviated. Modern lexical corroboration only: Interior Guider's “Banco Tanho” describes its bunho-fibre stool (https://interiorguider.com/tanho-stool/); it does not determine this transcription. Sanuqi is an upright name embedded in Portuguese.

Yamano iye means a mountain house. The Portuguese begins “a house that is in the mountains”; the initial Y, rather than OCR V, is visible. The accented està and the physical division mon-/tes are retained.
Completes montes from the preceding row and adds “or in the fields.” This is still the explanation of Sanxa, not an independent entry; the whole continuation is italic.
Yamagaua identifies a mountain river. The Portuguese offers streams or rivers and leaves its relative clause to the next line; the upright Japanese and italic explanation remain distinct.

The rivers in the preceding Sanxen entry “come from the mountains.” The unaccented printed vem is retained rather than modernizing the plural form; this short italic continuation is a complete physical row.
A different Sanxen is glossed by Yamano xemi, a woodland cicada. Portuguese cegarrega supplies the same insect sense. The Japanese xemi is not an OCR error for a modern s-spelling.
Yamano yuqi and the Portuguese both mean mountain snow. Sanxet retains its bare final t, and Neue retains the historical u/v spelling; neither is expanded or modernized.
Yamanoichi identifies a mountain market. The Portuguese starts “a fair held in the mountains.” The scan's joined Yamanoichi is retained, independently of the semantic boundary before ichi.

Finishes the market definition and introduces Sanxino xeiran as an example, then begins “one of the” celebrated views. The nasal abbreviation in Hũa and italic Vt are visible; the Japanese example remains upright.

runs.text: oito viſtas celebradas na China. Vide Facqei.

lines.note: Completes the description as one of eight celebrated Chinese views and directs the reader to Facqei. The cross-reference is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese apparatus; its locally italic appearance is preserved.
Sanxô is defined as a kind of Japanese pepper. The circumflex distinguishes the written headword form; the gloss does not warrant inserting a modern botanical name into the transcription.

This homograph denotes three bodily regions, followed by their Japanese names. The scan has Chǔ, not bare Chi, at the right edge, and no secure terminal hyphen. The printed S. is retained within the italic explanatory run rather than silently reinterpreted as a different abbreviation.

Completes Chǔxô across the physical break and adds Guexô; these are names in the Portuguese enumeration, not a standalone Japanese sentence. The following gloss begins with the upper parts, from the chest upward.

runs.text: pera cima, partes do meo, & partes inferiores.

lines.note: Completes the upper-region description and enumerates middle and lower parts. The scan reads inferiores, correcting OCR inſernores; historical pera and meo remain unchanged.

Yamano iro means the colour of the mountains, matching Portuguese cor dos montes. The visibly close printed Cordos is preserved; the terminal upright S. marks a written-language use and is separated from the italic gloss.
Yama and no are mountains and fields, exactly the two elements of the Portuguese definition. The comma between the Japanese gloss words belongs to the print and is not a word-joining instruction.
This Sanya instead concerns childbirth: Vmaruru iye is explained as a house of delivery or birth. The printed nacimento divides after na-; the Japanese initial V is retained.

Finishes the printed nacimento from the preceding line and gives Goſanya as the customary respectful expression. The enlarged scan resolves cimento, rather than OCR cimemo, and Ordinariamente; the punctuation after diz is a comma, and Goſanya is wholly upright with a final period.

The respectful Goſanya is used when speaking of a noble person. The separate far-right San- repeats the beginning of the following page and has been moved to a catchword zone, rather than treated as part of this definition. The existing provisional double-s expansion in peſſoa is retained.
